sentences.english: I. Account of the American languages in the manner and procedure of their operation.

The same mental process undeniably recurs in every language; its powers, means and results resemble and differ from one another as much as the diversity of human bodily and mental dispositions for language permits within the limits set by nature.

Whenever one attempts to describe particular languages, one must therefore start from the general type of this process and return to it, since otherwise the necessary point of comparison would be entirely lacking.

The generality of this type consists in everything that can be said of it being determined solely by the pure concept of language, with all other circumstances left aside: circumstances which arise from the other human dispositions and the conditions acting upon them, and which in reality individualise the general type.
What has so far been developed in this sense under the name of general grammar falls far short of exhausting the concept, stopping instead at a small part of it.

This discipline, which we unfortunately do not yet know whether the Indian grammarians had already advanced, but which the Greek grammarians brought in some respects to a perfection that left little to add, is actually concerned only with the logical analysis of discourse and the investigation of the word forms needed to connect thoughts within it; thus, in the first instance, with a product of language, and consequently with only a part of language.

Here and there, admittedly, the concept of general grammar has been given a wider scope; but nowhere, to my knowledge, has anyone attempted what is required here: an analysis of the procedure of language in the full interplay of its operations.

Since general grammar is also chiefly concerned with examining grammatical forms individually as the components of discourse, it falls largely within the following section under the quite different division of linguistic analysis attempted here, and can in no way relieve us of the task of establishing afresh, through the development of our own ideas, the general principles needed to compare particulars, however much better it would be, when describing a class of particular languages, to be able to refer to an established and tested general system of linguistic doctrine already constructed elsewhere.

Our immediate task must therefore be to sketch the general type of language, at least in its basic features, and then to examine what division of the whole subject matter to be treated in this chapter might follow from it.
A. Basic features of the general type of language.
a. The nature of language in general.

The mental process of language is taken here in its widest scope, not merely in language's relation to discourse and its stock of word elements, but also in relation to its influence on the capacities for thinking and feeling.

We consider the entire course by which language, proceeding from the mind, acts back upon the mind: in the individual, in the generation living at any given time, and in the nation across several generations.

For it has already been demonstrated elsewhere, and may surely be accepted as undisputed, that language is not merely the designation of thought formed independently of it, but is itself the formative organ of thought.

Intellectual activity, wholly mental, wholly inward, and in a sense passing without a trace, becomes outward and perceptible to the senses through sound in speech, and acquires an enduring body through writing.

What is produced in this way is everything spoken and recorded; language, however, is the totality of the sounds that the particular intellectual activity to which it belongs can produce by this means, together with their possible combinations and transformations according to laws which in turn arise from the nature of intellectual activity and its corresponding sound system.
Intellectual activity and language are therefore one and inseparable from each other; one cannot even regard the former simply as what produces and the latter as what is produced.

For although what is spoken on any occasion is certainly a product of the mind, it nevertheless belongs to a language already in existence, and is therefore determined not only by the mind's activity but also by the sounds and laws of that language; and as it immediately passes back into language as a whole, it acts back upon the mind, determining it in turn.
Intellectual activity is bound by the necessity of entering into a connection with sound; otherwise thinking cannot attain distinctness, nor can a representation become a concept.

It produces sound by a free decision and shapes it through its power, for sound becomes articulated sound through being permeated by intellectual activity; and it establishes a domain of such sounds which acts back upon it independently, determining and limiting it—if it were possible to conceive of a beginning of all language.

What thinking requires in language is not, strictly speaking, what is actually audible to the ear; or, to put it differently, if articulated sound is divided into articulation and noise, it requires only the former, not the latter.
Articulation rests on the mind's power over the organs of speech, compelling them to handle sound in a way corresponding to the form of its own operation.

The point at which this form and articulation meet, as in a connecting medium, is that both divide their domain into basic parts whose combination produces nothing but wholes that carry within themselves the striving to become parts of new wholes.

Besides this power, however, the mind also contains an impulse to make such use of the organs of speech, an impulse which communicates itself to those organs; and the production of language rests on this power and this impulse even independently of noise audible to the ear.
The example of deaf-mute people teaches us that language really is wholly inward and remains possible even without the production and perception of sound.

Every avenue of access to them through the ear is closed, yet they learn to understand what is spoken through the movements of the speaker's organs of speech and through writing; they themselves speak when the position and movement of their organs of speech are guided.

This can happen only through the capacity for articulation that they too possess: because of the connection between their thinking and their organs of speech, they learn to infer in another person one member of the connection, his thinking, from the other, the movement of his organs of speech.
The sound we hear reveals itself to them through the position and movement of the organs; they perceive its articulation without its noise.

Something sensory of which we have no conception may correspond to this noise in them too, perhaps something their imagination supplies in place of what is missing; but in any event, a remarkable separation of the components of articulated sound takes place in them.
They really understand language, since they learn to read and write alphabetically and even to speak, rather than merely understanding thought through signs or pictures.

They learn this not merely because they possess reason like other human beings, but quite specifically because they also possess a capacity for language: a correspondence between their thinking and their organs of speech, and an impulse to make the two work together, both essentially grounded in human nature, even though it is mutilated in one respect.

In the foregoing, however, articulation—whose concept I take here only in terms of its effect, as the shaping of sound that makes it a vehicle of thoughts—has been described only in its logical, or at least only in its intellectual, nature.
In its essential nature, however, it depends precisely on sound as noise, or rather on the vibration of the air through which the organs of speech act at a distance.

It can therefore never be applied directly to any sense other than hearing; however one attempted this, one would always produce only signs of sounds, not direct signs of words divisible into elementary parts.

This rests on the fact that precisely the vibration of the air, audible to another's ear and produced by organs determined by thought, is inseparably connected with human nature and necessary to its development.
Three things are involved here: thought's impulse towards expression, feeling's need to issue in an animal cry, and the necessity of social interaction for the development of thought.
Each of these leads separately to the production of sound, and language unites them all in articulated sound.
Thinking is a mental act, but through its need for language it becomes an impulse towards a bodily act.

It is a progressive unfolding, a purely inward movement in which nothing enduring, constant or at rest can be assumed, and at the same time a longing to pass from darkness into light, from limitation into infinity.

In the human being, whose twofold nature is fused into one, this striving also turns outwards and, through the mediation of the organs of speech, finds a material wonderfully suited to it in air, the finest and most easily moved of all the elements, whose apparent incorporeality corresponds to the mind even in sensory terms: a material in which, given the human upright posture, speech flows freely and calmly from the lips to the ear, which brings us the light of the stars, and which extends without visible bounds into infinity.
As mental striving thus breaks a path through the lips, its product returns to one's own ear; the subjective inward act is received again as an outward object.
Language thereby shares in and furthers the innermost essence of thinking: the constant passage of subject and object into each other.
For no kind of representation can be regarded as the mere contemplation of an object already present.

The activity of the senses must unite synthetically with the inward act of the mind; the representation breaks free from this union, becomes an object confronting the subjective power, and returns to that power when perceived anew as such an object.
Thus, quite apart from any communication between one human being and another, speaking is a necessary condition of the individual's thinking in secluded solitude.
In its actual manifestation, however, language develops only socially.
For a human being understands himself only after experimentally testing the intelligibility of his words on others.

When unarticulated sound takes the place of language, as it always does in animals and sometimes in human beings, either distress forces it out, as with painful feelings; or it has an intention behind it, as when it lures, warns or calls for help; or, without distress or intention, it pours forth from the joyful feeling of existence, from pleasure in the pealing of sounds.
The last is the poetic element, a spark flaring up in animal dullness.
These different kinds of sound are distributed very unequally among the more or less silent or richly vocal kinds of animal, and comparatively few have been granted the higher and more joyful kind.
To discover the source of this difference would be instructive for language too, but perhaps impossible.

The fact that birds alone possess song might perhaps be explained by their living more freely than all other animals in the element of sound, and in its purer regions, were it not that so many kinds of bird, like the animals that walk on the earth, are restricted to a few monotonous sounds.
The same impelling causes pass into language: distress, intention and pleasure in discourse.
But in language the last also refers, and chiefly, to thought, and this adds a fourth cause: the need to communicate and develop ideas and feelings through conversation.
It is surely among the most erroneous assertions to attribute the origin of languages chiefly to the need for mutual assistance.
Human beings in the state of nature are not so needy, and unarticulated sounds would have sufficed for that purpose, as we see in animals.
Language, even in its beginnings, is thoroughly human.

Even the languages of the so-called savages—indeed, precisely those languages—possess an abundance and variety of expressions everywhere exceeding need, and there is probably no wandering family in any wilderness that does not possess its songs; for the human being, considered as an animal species, is essentially a singing creature, only one that connects ideas with sounds.

The much more essential ground of language's origin is pleasure in speaking, and this is why the degree to which a people is taciturn or talkative has so important an influence on the formation of languages.

Even in their noblest endeavours, human beings must always be considered in their whole nature, one side of which they share with animality; hence we must not overlook in language the mere sounding through which animal sound passes, as it were, into articulated sound.
What first deserves attention here is the relation of this sounding to the designation of ideas.
It may be compared with colouring in painting.
Languages are sometimes richer, sometimes poorer in it, sometimes freer from pealing noise, sometimes more overloaded with it.

But languages also sometimes, either generally or at certain stages of development, mix more or less thoughtless pealing into actual language, using syllables and even words without any definite effect on the meaning, almost solely to fill out the sound.
Some feeling may admittedly attach to everything of this kind, but that is possible with unarticulated sound too.
As language is cultivated, these mere filler words either disappear or, in the more favourable case, become signs of fine nuances of ideas or their connections through more skilful elaboration.
Ultimately, the true individuality of each language lies solely in the nature of sound as such.

Whatever one does or attempts in describing its peculiarities, one only defines more and more closely the class to which it belongs; as this language and no other, it expresses itself only by sounding itself before the ear.

Although the alphabet of all humanity is confined within certain limits, which are not even very wide, every people with a language of its own nevertheless also has its own sound system: in excluding certain sounds, preferring others, assigning different sounds to designate different concepts, handling sounds in their combinations, and so forth.
This may be compared with the different cries and vocal modes of the kinds of animal.

Although progressive development brings much to completion, there is nevertheless something fixed and characteristic of a stock in this, deeply grounded in modifications of the organs of speech and in the feeling for sound.

It distinguishes stocks even more than languages, however, since within the same language particular stocks have sounds entirely different from those of all the others, as the Florentines, for example, have their aspirated guttural.

Yet apart from such details, which seem accidental to language in itself, the sound system has the most significant influence on the most essential parts of every language; it is the first thing in which one must establish a thoroughly firm footing.

Admittedly, this leads into laborious elementary investigation, often descending to minutiae; but the total impression of languages rests entirely on details that are minute in themselves, and nothing is more incompatible with studying languages than wanting to seek in them only what is great, mental and predominant.

Close attention to every grammatical subtlety, and the splitting of words into their elements, are absolutely necessary if one is to avoid exposing every judgement about structure, and even about descent, to error.
The most important reason why language needs to act outwards through sound is sociability, towards which human beings are unconditionally directed by their nature.

Sociability contains two things, though they are closely connected in a third, higher one: first, that all human powers develop fully only in society; and second, that there is something common to the whole human race, of which each individual possesses a particular determination carrying within it the desire to be completed by the others.
Both are especially important precisely in language.

For the greater and more animated the social interplay acting upon language, the more it gains, other circumstances being equal; and the possibility of all understanding rests on the common element just mentioned.
Sociability too cannot be derived from mere need without one-sidedness.
It does not rest on need even in animals.
Scarcely any animal is so self-sufficient in its strength as the elephant, which nevertheless lives predominantly in herds.
Thus in animals too, the greater inclination towards sociability in some kinds and the lesser inclination in others arise from causes lying much deeper in their being.
It is simply impossible for us to fathom these causes, because we can form no conception at all of animals' nevertheless undeniable ability to perceive, to feel and to connect perceptions.

In human beings, however, thinking is essentially bound to social existence; quite apart from all bodily relations and relations of feeling, a human being needs, simply in order to think, a You corresponding to the I: a concept attains its definiteness and clarity only by being reflected back from another power of thought.
It is produced by breaking free from the moving mass of representation and forming itself into an object confronting the subject.

Yet it is not enough for this division to take place within the subject alone; objectivity is complete only when the person forming representations actually sees the thought outside himself, which is possible only in another being that forms representations and thinks as he does.
But language is the sole mediator between one power of thought and another, and so here too its necessity for the completion of thought becomes apparent.
There is also an unalterable dualism within language itself, and all speaking is directed towards address and reply.
The word is not a thing; rather, in relation to things it is something subjective, yet in the mind of the thinker it is nevertheless to be an object, produced by him and acting back upon him.
To distinguish itself from a merely apparent object, a dream image, it must acquire substantial reality in someone who hears and replies.
The pronoun expresses this original type of all languages by distinguishing the second person from the third.
I and He are genuinely different objects, and in fact they exhaust everything, for in other words they mean I and Not-I.
You, however, is a He placed opposite the I.
Whereas I and He rest on inward and outward perception, You involves spontaneity of choice.
It too is a Not-I, but unlike He it lies not in the sphere of all beings, but in another sphere, that of action made common through influence.
He itself thereby comes to contain, besides Not-I, also Not-You, and is opposed not merely to one of them but to both.

The fact that the same pronominal form runs through all languages shows that, according to the feeling of all peoples, speaking essentially presupposes that the speaker distinguishes, opposite himself, an addressee from everyone else.

Several American languages even show particular care in singling out the second person by indicating, through different forms in the first-person plural as well, whether the addressee is included or excluded.
What emerges in this way when we attempt to analyse the simple act of thinking repeats itself unceasingly in human mental life; social communication affords conviction and stimulation.
The power of thought needs something like itself and yet distinct from itself.
It is kindled by what is like itself, while what is distinct from it supplies a touchstone for the substantial reality of its inward productions.

For in his changeable limitation, the human being can regard truth, as what is boundlessly fixed, only as something lying outside himself; all his mental striving is a struggle towards it, and social association is the most powerful means of approaching it and measuring his distance from it.
Language is thus a necessary requirement both for the first production of thought and for the progressive development of the mind.
Mental communication, in passing from one person to another, presupposes in the latter something he has in common with the former.
We understand a word we hear only because we could have said it ourselves.

Nothing can be present in the soul except through its own activity, and understanding, just as much as speaking, is itself a stimulation of the power of language, only in its inward receptivity, as speaking is in its outward activity; hence it is also so natural for human beings immediately to say again what they have just understood.

Language therefore lies within every human being in its entire extent; but this means nothing other than that everyone possesses a striving, regulated through the prompting and limiting action of a specifically modified power, gradually to produce the whole language, or to understand it when produced, as inward or outward occasions arise.

Like every power, this is naturally an individual one, but it is individualised according to all those concepts of classes by virtue of which each class can be taken as an individual in relation to a higher, more general class.

It is thus the general power of language, determined by the ethnic stock, the nation and the dialect; then, with its sound signs fixed, determined in its manner of use by all the inward qualities and outward contingencies that act upon the mind so powerfully that their effect becomes perceptible in language; and finally determined by the individuality that can no longer be brought under any more general category.
Each of these levels, ascending to the most general, forms a linguistic sphere determined by what is common to everything included within it and by what distinguishes it from everything outside it.

In every general investigation of language it therefore becomes necessary, at the various points under consideration—for example, the alphabet—to seek the limits of human language in general, to distinguish within this wide domain the smaller, again mutually nested domains of particular classes of language, and everywhere to consider whether these fulfil the concept from which the division was made, and thus form in their historical existence a whole given by the idea.

Every multiplicity of things alike in kind brings this task with it, especially in investigations which, like those concerning language, are conducted not merely to gain and present historical knowledge, but teleologically to act back formatively upon language and human beings.
The general interconnectedness of languages is certainly explained by the likeness in kind of human nature, in which similar powers operate according to the same laws.

Yet a deeper investigation and fuller appreciation of language seem to me to lead much further, to a point towards which I have so far sought to prepare the way only through less demanding reflections, and at which no further explanation is possible; for no metaphysical investigation—that is, one grounded in fathoming being in itself—can lead beyond the point where what is to be explained ends.

To me—for I prefer to express this in the tone of inward conviction rather than with the assurance of a universal assertion—the essence of language seems to be misunderstood, the mental process of its genesis—not that in itself, but also that in each act of speaking and understanding—only seemingly explained, and its powerful influence on the mind incorrectly appreciated, if the human race is regarded as countless natures belonging to the same species, rather than as one nature divided into countless individuals: a view reached in quite other connections than that of language, and from quite different starting points.

The difference between the two opposed assertions is evident, since on the latter view the inward kinship of the human race rests on the unity of its being, whereas on the former it rests only on the unity of the idea that encompasses it, whether in contemplation or in creation.
The nature of this kinship holds the secret of human individuality, which may also be regarded as the secret of human existence.

This is the point at which one might especially expect a difference in a state following earthly life, a difference which, if consciousness linked the two states, would at the same time bring about a complete transformation of all previous views.

This secret cannot be explained or fathomed; but to explain phenomena correctly and give direction to intellectual striving, we must guard against misunderstanding the true essence of that kinship of human individuality, against deriving it merely from logical and discursive concepts, rather than grasping it from the depths of inward feeling and through reflection that pursues the investigation to its furthest points.
Something is therefore already gained if we leave the view identified above as correct standing even as a dimly apprehended possibility, so as not to shut ourselves within the opposite view.

What speaks most convincingly against that opposite view for me is what was said above: that understanding too rests entirely on inward self-activity, and speaking with one another is merely a mutual awakening of the power of language present in the hearer.
Comprehending words is something entirely different from understanding unarticulated sounds, and involves far more than the mere reciprocal evocation of the sound and the object indicated.

A word can certainly also be taken as an indivisible whole, just as in writing one may recognise the sense of a group of words without yet being sure of its alphabetic composition; and it would be possible for a child's soul to proceed in this way in the earliest beginnings of understanding.

But as soon as not merely the animal capacity for feeling but the human power of language is stimulated—and there may well be no moment even in the child when this is not the case, however faintly—the word is also perceived as articulated.

What articulation adds to the mere evocation of the word's meaning—which it naturally also accomplishes more perfectly—is that through its form it immediately presents the word as part of an infinite whole, a language.

For articulation provides, even in individual words, the possibility of forming from their elements a number of other words that genuinely extends to infinity, according to determining feelings and rules, and thereby of establishing among all words a kinship corresponding to the kinship of concepts.

The soul would have no inkling of this skilfully contrived mechanism, and would comprehend articulation no more than a blind person comprehends colour, unless it possessed a power to turn that possibility into actuality.
Children's learning to speak is not a matter of words being portioned out, deposited in memory and babbled back with the lips, but a growth of the capacity for language through age and practice.

What is heard does more than merely communicate itself: it prepares the soul to understand more easily even what has not yet been heard; it clarifies things heard long ago but then understood only partly or not at all, as their likeness in kind to what has just been perceived suddenly becomes evident to a power that has since grown more acute; and it sharpens the impulse and ability to draw ever more of what is heard, and ever more quickly, into understanding, allowing ever less of it to rush past as mere sound.

Progress therefore does not occur, as in learning vocabulary, at a steady rate increasing only through greater exercise of memory, but at a rate that constantly increases of itself, since the enhancement of the power and the acquisition of material mutually strengthen and extend each other.

That children undergo a development of the power of language rather than mechanically learning language is also shown by the fact that all human powers are assigned a certain period of life for their development, and that under the most varied circumstances all children speak and understand at approximately the same age, varying only within a short span.

But how could the hearer, merely through the growth of his developing power, acquire such strength to master what is spoken, unless the same being were present in speaker and hearer, divided only individually and in ways suited to each other, so that a sign as subtle as articulated sound, yet drawn precisely from the deepest and fullest nature of that being, suffices to mediate between them and stimulate both in a corresponding manner?
If this is correct, it also becomes clear how the separation and intermingling of nations cause the diversity of their languages.

For the further human beings diverge through these processes, the more the separation of individuality opposes the unity of being, although the unity of human nature in general is also demonstrated by the fact that children of any people, transferred from the womb into any foreign people, develop their capacity for language in that people's language.

This phenomenon can admittedly also be cited in support of the exact opposite position: that speaking is merely a reproduction of what is heard and depends on social intercourse, irrespective of unity or diversity of being.

But however much must be attributed to the power, even the predominant power, of the surrounding sounds, it would be arbitrary to deny the influence of descent, which in these exceptional cases is merely suppressed.

Descent already exercises an undeniable influence on the vocal organs, which must be individually modified, naturally in accordance with the language of the fathers, and which now, in accommodating and resisting, mingle this modification into every influence acting upon them.
Nothing in a human being is so isolated, however, and the intellectual capacity for language certainly also possesses a similar disposition characteristic of the stock.

The fact that the native language possesses much greater force and intimacy than a foreign one for educated and uneducated people alike; that after long deprivation it greets the ear with a kind of sudden enchantment and, far from home, touches one with longing; and that this rests not at all on its mental content, the thought or feeling expressed, but precisely on what is inexplicable and most individual, its sound—this too might well speak for that actual unity of being.
It is as though in the familiar sound one heard a part of oneself coming from the other person.

If only sufficient attention is paid to phenomena of this kind, one can also point out, in the finest and most intellectual use of language, in the literatures of nations, individuals who, estranged from childhood from their own language, which they never learnt at all, nevertheless always mingled something into their use of the language they acquired that showed how their original destination for another language had been accidentally displaced, contrary to the nature of their being.
Nevertheless, distinctive dialects arise even without any influence of descent, merely through intercourse and shared life.

This is found especially among particular classes of the people within the sphere of actual national languages; the distinctive dialects of women, so frequent particularly in American languages, and those of the different social ranks in Malay are of this kind.
Common descent may also be added, however, as in the language of the Incas, which was both a family language and the language of a social rank.
In all these cases, as in the formation of language generally, the principle is a community that separates itself, accidentally or deliberately.
In presenting language above as the organ of thinking, we considered articulated sound, which constitutes its essence, in its twofold nature: as articulation (21) and as sound (22–38).

If we now turn to what is produced through speaking, or rather through thinking in language, we find here too that the view that language merely designates perceived objects, whose totality we call the world, is far from exhausting its deep and full content.
Just as no concept is possible without language, neither can any object exist for the soul without it, since every external object acquires substantial reality for the soul only through the concept.
The entire manner of the subjective perception of objects necessarily enters into the formation and use of language.
For the word arises from this perception and is an imprint not of the object in itself, but of the image produced by it in the soul.

Since subjectivity is inevitably mingled into every objective perception, each human individuality can already be regarded, independently of language, as a distinctive standpoint for a view of the world.

Language makes it so to a much greater degree, however, since the word in turn makes itself an object confronting the soul and adds a new peculiarity that separates itself from the subject; the concept thus now contains three things: the impression of the object, the manner in which the subject receives it, and the effect of the word as a speech sound.

Within the same language, a pervasive analogy necessarily governs this last effect; and since a subjectivity alike in kind also acts upon language within the same nation, each language contains a distinctive view of the world.
This expression in no way exceeds the measure of plain truth.

For the connection of all the parts of language with one another, and of the whole language with the nation, is so close that once this interaction takes a definite direction, a pervasive distinctive character must necessarily follow.

Language is a view of the world not merely because, since every concept must be capable of being grasped through it, it must equal the world in scope, but also because only the transformation it performs upon objects enables the mind to apprehend the interconnectedness inseparable from the concept of the world.
Human beings also live chiefly with objects as language presents them to them, and, since their feeling and acting depend on their representations, indeed exclusively so.

Through the very act by which the human being spins language out of himself, he spins himself into it; and every language draws a circle around the nation to which it belongs, a circle that can be left only to the extent that one simultaneously passes into the circle of another language.

Learning a foreign language, when put to proper use, is therefore the acquisition of a new standpoint within one's previous view of the world, since each language contains the entire fabric of concepts and manner of representation of a portion of humanity.
So far I have dealt more with speaking than with language, chiefly describing the production and understanding of discourse and the influence it exercises on the soul.

Yet language is produced from speaking, a stock of words and a system of rules, and, winding its way through successive millennia, grows into a power in some respects independent of the particular speaker, the particular generation, the nation, and ultimately even humanity itself.
We noted above that thought taken up into language becomes an object for the soul and exercises an effect upon it which, in this respect, comes to it as something alien.
But we considered the object chiefly as arising from the subject, and the effect as proceeding from that upon which it acts back.
The opposite view now comes into play, according to which language really is an alien object and its effect really does proceed from something other than that upon which it acts.

For language must necessarily belong to two people (31), and in fact belongs to the whole human race; since in writing it also preserves slumbering thought so that the mind can awaken it, it forms for itself a distinctive existence which can admittedly become effective only in particular acts of thinking, but which in its totality is independent of them.

The two opposed views raised here—that language is alien to the soul and belongs to it, is independent of it and dependent upon it—really are united in language and constitute the peculiarity of its essence.
Nor should this conflict be resolved by saying that language is partly alien and independent and partly neither.
Language is an object and self-subsistent precisely insofar as it is a subject and dependent.

For it has no permanent abode anywhere, not even in writing, but must always be produced anew in thinking and consequently pass wholly into the subject; yet the very act of producing it involves making it equally an object; in this way it receives the individual's full influence on each occasion, but that influence is already inherently constrained by what language does and has done.
The true resolution of this opposition lies in the unity of human nature mentioned above (34).
In what proceeds from that which is actually one with me, the concepts of subject and object, dependence and independence, pass into one another.
Language belongs to me because I produce it.

It does not belong to me because I cannot produce it otherwise than I do; and since the ground of this lies in the speaking and past speaking of all human generations, insofar as linguistic communication may have continued uninterrupted among them, it is language itself that imposes this restriction upon me.

Besides the influence of language just mentioned, the alien influence to which human beings are subject in using language also includes, given its close connection with the whole of their remaining being, the influence exercised upon that being by descent, surrounding circumstances and the manner of shared life.

This is especially important in historical investigations of language, since on the one hand we must guard against explaining a language entirely from the circumstances acting upon the nation, and on the other must not forget that even a language undeniably handed down in history can undergo seemingly incredible modifications through the nation.
Everywhere in linguistic investigations we have to deal with this twofold series of interconnected effects.

For, like all investigations concerning the human race historically, they always place us only in the midst of things; to try to conceive of a beginning, let alone explain one, would lead to empty suppositions.

Even where neither history nor tradition gives knowledge of an earlier state or reveals a wider connection, we must therefore always regard finding some such connection as a task for an attention directed everywhere.

If we consider how everything a people's language has experienced throughout all preceding centuries acts constrainingly upon each successive generation, and how only the power of the single generation comes into contact with this—and not even that in isolation, since the rising and departing generations live intermingled alongside one another—it becomes clear how small the individual's power really is beside the power of language.

The balance is restored to some degree only through language's extraordinary plasticity, through the possibility, which I shall discuss below, of taking its forms in very different ways without impairing general understanding, and through the power that everything mentally alive exercises over what is handed down dead.
Yet it is always in language that each individual feels himself to be nothing but an outflow of the whole human race.
Nevertheless, because everyone individually and unceasingly acts back upon language, each generation produces a change in it, which only in many cases escapes observation.

For change can be of two kinds: a change in the words and forms themselves, and a change in their differently modified use; where writing and literature are absent, the latter is both less extensive and harder to perceive.

Since only what already exists is ever changed, and always only by a single power struggling against an infinite mass, it follows of itself that every change in language, and the emergence of new languages too, occurs only gradually.

Nations too, which go hand in hand with languages through the changing centuries, arise in no other way; and the means by which all new languages are formed, insofar as we can discern them, are estrangement and admixture.
A group branches off from a stock and settles where it either encounters no one as yet or intermingles with another stock.

Within historical investigation of language there can be no question of the invention of a language; and the expressions that a people creates its language, that language proceeds from its individuality, even that language belongs exclusively to it, require caution if they are to be used correctly.

The same applies to using the concept of descent for languages: it must never be taken to mean that one language could proceed in its totality from another, but only that the supposed mother language has been transformed into a daughter language in the mouths of generations that separated themselves and intermingled with foreign ones.

But since in this way several languages pass into a new one, applying this concept already misleads by prompting a search for one ancestral language, when all the different materials of the language under investigation ought to be distinguished.

Nations themselves are no more cleanly separated from one another, but likewise flow into one another and gradually form through the conjoint principle of separation and holding together; only at a certain point, once formation is complete, does the distinctive character arising in this way become visible.
Mr Klaproth already makes this observation in Asia polyglotta, p. [43.]
All the languages of peoples between whom any connection has ever existed must therefore be regarded as one language, modified into manifold varieties only through estrangement and intermingling.

This is a fundamental principle in every investigation of language, equally important for examining the likeness in kind of languages etymologically and for presenting philosophically the manner in which language spreads across the human race.

It rests, however, on the simple and undeniable fact that where people who previously lived entirely apart visit or join with one another, [they] gradually modify their original speaking and transform it into a new manner of speaking on which they converge—usually both parties do so, though sometimes only one, overcome by the other first physically and then mentally.
Even where the original manners of speaking remain separate, individual words and forms nevertheless pass back and forth.
We must therefore seek out etymologically the different elements of the language and their relation to one another.

Only if all the elements were alike in kind and agreed with the language of another people—that is, if the language had arisen solely through branching off, without any mixture—could the concept of descent fit.
But since this concept always also entails earlier and later existence, the question of descent can almost never be decided from language alone.
Philosophically, the task is now to investigate what human beings hold to most firmly in language, and what kinds of diversity they enter into more readily or with greater difficulty.

The unity of several languages expressed in the principle just established by no means signifies the unity of a primordial language; rather, it means that each contains some element also belonging to another, and that, since this is true of all, all are indirectly modified and affected by one another.

What is distinctive about that assertion is that it regards the different languages as coexisting parts or dialects of one language embracing them all, rather than as having arisen from one another in time; moreover, it makes no claim to novelty, but aims only, by cutting away inappropriate analogies, to define the concepts more firmly and bring them into closer agreement with the facts.

The temporal succession of languages must not be neglected in studying them either; it should simply not be introduced inappropriately, and since the beginnings of most languages still existing are lost in darkness, our ignorance of their temporal succession makes them in a sense simultaneous for us.
To assume a primordial language, or to posit a difference between languages before and after the destruction of the greater part of the human race by a flood, seems to me useless and misleading.
Neither the domain of facts nor that of pure concepts can lead us there.

There may have been one primordial language, or several: in the strictest sense, if the human race had more than one geographical point of origin; in a less strict sense, if peoples had become so isolated—and great floods in particular could bring this about—that every trace of their earlier connection had been lost in their language.
Yet facts drawn from languages will scarcely prove either possibility, and explaining phenomena in language will scarcely require either assumption.

Nevertheless, provided one intends to infer nothing particular from it, the concept of a primordial language can certainly no more be rejected than that of any beginning of the human race; and thus, in relation to the principle established above (44), it may also happen that a group which has branched off from a people intermingles with another group upon which none of the languages connected with the first has ever exercised any influence, even in the most indirect way.
Two such ethnic stocks would then, if the succession of generations were traced backwards, indeed connect their languages to two primordial languages.

Wherever actual intercourse between speakers has existed among peoples, however indirectly, likeness in kind between their languages arises from language already formed; conversely, if such likeness in kind arising from formed language can be recognised in languages, it proves such intercourse.

This is important because it at least states the principle by which the historical connection between languages can be distinguished from the likeness in kind to be sought solely in the likeness in kind of human dispositions, even if the principle should prove of little practical fruitfulness.

For suppose that the American nations had originated in their own homeland and had not intermingled with any inhabitants of the rest of the earth before the spread of the languages still existing: no non-American sound would then have been heard in America, and there could be no likeness in kind between American languages and the other languages of the earth arising through language already formed.

Nevertheless, the general human dispositions would still be the same in America too; whether one derived them from descent from a single human pair or from the unity of the creative idea, there would be the same unity of human being without which (34) language itself would be impossible, and a likeness in kind between languages would therefore necessarily have to arise from this too.
In this sense there is only one language, just as there is only one human species, and no difference of races annuls either the concept of humanity or the possibility of regular reproduction.

This becomes still more evident when we consider that the natural surroundings acting upon human beings, and consequently upon language too, are broadly the same, and that the means employed by all languages, namely sounds, are confined within limits that are not very wide.

This general likeness in kind also occurs in historically connected languages, but only in the parts upon which the sounds introduced from outside have not acted, and never in a pure form, since in language, which exists only in the activity of producing it on each occasion (40), every influence always permeates the whole.

Whether there may be sufficient means of distinguishing these two possible kinds of likeness in the languages themselves may be left undecided for now; but it was necessary to define them precisely in conceptual terms.

We shall have to return to this point at great length later, since America could more readily have remained free of all intermingling with foreigners than any part of the Old World, unless one wished perhaps to except central Africa.
We therefore encounter things alike in kind in all languages, and the hope of finding something entirely new in any one of them would be vain.
I do not deny that the great similarity between the European and several Asian languages first drove me to study the American languages.
I thought I would enter an entirely foreign domain there, and at first sight, and in a certain respect, this is indeed so; but closer examination shows the phenomena there too to be less alien.
The task in investigating each language is therefore to recognise what is characteristic within likeness in kind.

For since language is always one—that is, since everything thought in language always proceeds from the individual's entire language, or, if this seems clearer, entire proficiency in language, at the particular moment, and consequently the entire language is imprinted in this single utterance—what is alike in kind does not merely exist alongside what is characteristic, but passes into it: that is, the general power dwelling within the whole human race determines itself individually.

Likeness in kind and individuality can therefore be separated only in the idea; and although the individual, as the immediate fact, can only be perceived, not analysed and presented to the understanding, we must nevertheless grasp the two in their unity as far as possible.

I should not wish what I have just said about the appearance of the entire language in each particular thing spoken to be taken for one of those exaggerations to which we easily risk surrendering ourselves in general reasonings devoid of examples.
What it is intended to express is that in language everything is determined by each thing and each thing by everything, and this is literally true.

Even in the simplest sentence, a large part of this interconnectedness can actually be demonstrated: one divides the sentence into its elements according to every kind of analysis possible in languages, places each element in all the categories appropriate to it, compares it there with the other elements included in the same category, then compares the categories themselves with one another, and continues in this way through all the determining relations of the language, investigating how the determination operative in each also determines the element of the given sentence.
Admittedly, however, infinitely much rests on analogies of the feeling for language that cannot be presented.

It follows of itself from the foregoing that, although the individual speech sound is the ultimate actual manifestation, the individuality of a language must not be sought solely in its sound, with likeness in kind assigned, perhaps, to its ideal content.
Rather, individuality manifests itself in everything, and is one and the same throughout the totality of the language, from its alphabet to its representation of the world (39).
If those basic sounds were differently constituted, this manner of apprehension would be different too, and conversely.
No one will demand that this should actually be demonstrated in any particular language.

That is certainly impossible, but the proposition is nevertheless true and important: true because it follows necessarily from the nature of speaking and language developed above; important because departing from the two fundamental truths of all linguistic investigation—that language is one with the whole of human thinking and feeling, and that it has no existence anywhere except in the eternally reciprocally productive act of speaking and thinking in language—departing, I say, from these truths also makes us overlook what can actually be known in existing languages.
Above all, a proper widening of our outlook on languages is necessary for treating them correctly.

Since everything in language is mental, the strength and fullness of its effect on thinking and feeling depend on the energy and intelligence that employ it; and every more accurate insight into language comes alive in the whole human being through the purer influence of its individuality.

In one's own use of language, however, everything that can never be presented by the analysing understanding also enters feeling and thus knowledge; hence a use guided by a wider overview also gives rise to wider insight.
Whatever one has felt in one's own language, however deep and subtle it may be, one more readily divines in a foreign one.

Thus it is surely undeniable that, since the principal nations of Europe began writing in their mother tongues, an entirely different insight has arisen into the interconnectedness of each language within itself and with its nation.

This too distinguishes that epoch, which I consider the most important in the treatment of language, and which exercises a much more powerful influence in our time than the same phenomenon did among the ancients, since among them only two languages came into contact, whereas among us several did, and in much more lively rivalry.

To leave nothing wanting in the precise delimitation of concepts, however, we must add to the foregoing that the individuality of a language can itself be individuality only comparatively, and that true individuality lies only in the person speaking on each occasion.
In fact, only this completes the concept.

A nation certainly has, on the whole, the same language; yet not even all its members have precisely the same one (38), and if we proceed further into the finest detail, each human being possesses a language of his own.

No one thinks exactly what another does on hearing a word, and the difference, however small, trembles through the entire language, if we may compare language with the most mobile of all the elements.
In every act of thinking and feeling, the same difference recurs by virtue of the sameness of the individuality, forming a mass out of things individually imperceptible.

All understanding is therefore always at the same time a not-understanding—a truth that can also be put to excellent use in practical life—and all agreement in thoughts and feelings is at the same time a divergence.

This remains invisible only where it hides beneath the generality of concept and feeling; but where heightened power breaks through that generality and individualises more sharply even for consciousness, it comes clearly to light.
Thus no one will deny that every significant writer has a language of his own.
It may admittedly be objected that by language we mean precisely that generality of forms, words and rules which allows room for diverse individuality, and this is certainly perfectly true.
Nevertheless, the view raised here cannot on that account be banished even from the domain of the most general investigation of language.

For there are several levels at which the generality of linguistic forms is individualised in this way, and the individualising principle is the same: thinking and speaking within a particular individuality.
This gives rise to diversity in the language of individuals as of nations.
Everywhere it is only a matter of more or less.
We must therefore descend to the final level.
One might admittedly wish to find the boundary where language, though individually nuanced, nevertheless employs the same sounds.

But even among the different classes of a nation this is not entirely the case; and the individual too uses some preferentially, employs others as though they were foreign to him, excludes still others altogether, and thereby forms his own dictionary, quite apart from divergences in meaning.

Above all, however, attention must be drawn to the modification of language in each individual, in order to demonstrate human power over language, just as we presented its power over human beings above (42, 43).

The latter may be regarded as a physiological operation, if one wishes to apply the expression to mental powers; the former is a purely dynamic operation: in the latter lies the nature of the operative powers of language, in the former the principle of their freedom.

For something may arise in a human being whose ground no understanding can discover in preceding states; and we would misunderstand the nature of language, and violate precisely the historical truth of its genesis and transformation, if we sought to exclude from it the possibility of such inexplicable phenomena.

Yet although freedom cannot be determined or explained, its limits can be recognised, albeit only within a certain latitude; linguistic investigation must recognise and honour the manifestation of freedom, but carefully trace its limits, so as not to regard as possible in languages through freedom what is not possible.

Nations also continually change their languages purely through themselves, without branching off or mixture, in the continuing course of their common life; these changes become perceptible after longer periods.
The extent, speed and manner of these transformations depend on the liveliness of linguistic intercourse and the depth with which human beings grasp the content of language.
For we shall see below that there are different degrees in this.
Attending to these transformations is a principal task of linguistic research.

But even where language is more violently reshaped through branching off and mixture, national individuality exercises a predominant influence according to the way the foreign element touches it and the way it works upon that element with its inherent power.

It scarcely needs recalling, however, that to make this national influence clear to ourselves, we must go back to the individual's distinctive treatment of language, which appears in that influence only in the aggregate.

Yet even within a nation, an individual sometimes departs from the course given by everyone and establishes a new way of treating language through an insight suddenly flashing upon him, through a decisive invention, or through his distinctive manner of using language.
For although limits are set to the intellectuality of nations, as to that of the human race, a certain latitude remains reserved for the individual even here.

Wherever freedom moves within the bounds of finitude, there is certainly a series of determining influences alien to it at the moment of action; yet, like lightning from a cloudless ether, it can also suddenly emerge from them and become self-determining.

On this rests the fact that an unceasing creation is alive in humanity and in the deeply stirred human being, and that the manner of their being can never be calculated or exhaustively explained, since the inexplicable principle of freedom remains mingled into every direction it takes.

In languages, this is why they unexpectedly take sudden flights upwards and do not even always decline gradually; why languages alike in kind in themselves receive such different treatment among different nations that they display great diversity of character, as Greek and Latin do, for example; and why individual writers inaugurate entirely new epochs in the manner of treating them—something that certainly also occurs before the invention of writing, but there is lost in darkness for posterity.

This consideration becomes especially important for linguistic research as a warning against treating merely mechanical modes of explanation as sufficient and placing excessive trust in analytical procedure.

Research must certainly trace the uniform course human beings take in transforming and forming language, but only with regard for the independent power capable of leaving that course or shortening it, whose mere breath gives linguistic materials an entirely different nature; one must certainly analyse and derive one thing from another, but only with the feeling that there are also true syntheses, in which idea and sound meet by a route that cannot be investigated further.

Just as the stock of words and system of rules we call language are always fertilised by the living mind in thinking, speaking and recording, so investigation too must always keep both the living mind and dead language in view and follow their interaction.
The individuality of nations can take such manifold paths that any attempt even to comprehend it in classes would be vain.

But for the principal influences on language, only two points ever matter: whether national individuality inclines towards intellectuality at all, and from what side; and whether it inclines specifically towards intellectuality through language.

For just as in daily life we encounter different degrees and kinds of need for language, feeling for language and treatment of language among individuals, so too with nations; and what manifests itself in the continual further development of languages also occurred in their emergence from one another, since this itself (43) could only have been a gradual becoming different.

Much more could be observed about this diversity in the national appropriation of language, were it not my purpose in this chapter to touch on particulars only by way of indication, in order to show the structure and interlocking of the whole.

Having now considered language in general in its twofold nature, as a mental act in speaking and understanding, and as dead material produced through that act, material which never exists outside human beings but always exists outside the individual (40–54); and having further distinguished within it the natural nexus (40–51) from national and individual freedom (52–54), we now turn to its procedure in detail.
Here two things clearly separate from one another: words and the connection of discourse, as the matter and form of language.

This division must not be confused with the division into sounds and rules, for word formation too has rules, and the connection of discourse sometimes employs sounds peculiar to it; rather, regarding discourse as the purpose of language, we must hold firmly to the true nature of this classification, so that one part treats the elements of discourse and the other their connection.
Since sound is common to both, however, an examination of the sound system must precede them.
