sentences.english: 1. Presentation of the American languages in the manner and according to the procedure of their working.

In every language the same mental process undeniably repeats itself; powers, means and results are as like and unlike one another as the human bodily and mental dispositions for language permit diversity within the limits set by nature.

Where one now attempts to describe individual languages, one must start from the general type of this process and return to it, because otherwise the necessary point of comparison would be entirely lacking.

The generality of this type consists in this, that everything that is to be asserted of it is conditioned only by the pure concept of language and that abstraction is made from all other circumstances which, arising from the remaining human dispositions and from the conditions acting upon them, individualize the general type in reality.
What has hitherto been worked out in this sense, under the name of general grammar, by no means exhausts the concept, but stops at a small part of it.

This science, of which we unfortunately do not yet know whether it had already made progress among the Indian grammarians, but which had been brought by the Greek grammarians in some points to a perfection that allowed little more to be added, is really concerned only with the logical analysis of speech and with the investigation of the word-forms necessary in it for connecting thoughts; thus in the first instance with a product of language and therefore only with a part of language.

A greater extension has indeed here and there been given to the concept of general grammar, but nowhere, so far as I know, has an analysis of the procedure of language in its whole joint working been attempted, as is required here.

Since it is also chiefly concerned in detail with considering the grammatical forms as the constituents of speech, it falls, according to the wholly different division of the analysis of language attempted here, for the most part into the following section, and can in no way relieve us of the task of setting up anew here, from our own development of ideas, the general element required for comparison of the particular, however much better it would be, in describing a genus of determinate languages, to be able to refer to a general system of doctrine concerning language already erected and proved elsewhere.

It will therefore now first be necessary to sketch the general type of language at least in its fundamental features, and then to examine what division of the whole material to be treated in this chapter is likely to result from it.
A. Fundamental features of the general type of language.
a. Nature of language in general.

The mental process of language is taken here in its widest extension, not merely in the relation of language to speech and to the stock of its word-elements, but also in its relation to its influence on the faculty of thought and feeling.

The whole course comes into consideration along which it, proceeding from the mind, reacts upon the mind, in the individual, in the generation living at any given time and in the nation through several generations.

For it has already been shown elsewhere, and may well be assumed as undisputed, that language is not merely the designation of thought formed independently of it, but is itself the formative organ of thought.

Intellectual activity, wholly mental, wholly inward, and in a certain measure passing without trace, becomes outward and perceptible to the senses through tone in speech, and receives through writing an enduring body.

What is produced in this way is what is spoken and recorded of every kind; language, however, is the totality of the sounds which the determinate intellectual activity to which it belongs is able to produce by this path, and of the combinations and transformations of them that are possible according to laws which in turn proceed from the nature of the intellectual activity and of the system of tones corresponding to it.
Intellectual activity and language are therefore one and inseparable from each other; one cannot even simply regard the former as what produces and the other as what is produced.

For although what is spoken at any given time is indeed a product of the mind, it is nevertheless, inasmuch as it belongs to the language already existing beforehand, determined, besides by the activity of the mind, by the sounds and laws of the language, and, inasmuch as it at once passes again into language in general, reacts in a determining way upon the mind.
Intellectual activity is bound to the necessity of entering into a combination with tone; otherwise thinking cannot attain distinctness, nor representation become concept.

It produces tone from free resolve and forms it by its power, for by virtue of its penetration of it tone becomes articulated sound (if it were possible to think a beginning of all language), and establishes a domain of such sounds which, independent, determining and limiting, reacts upon it.

That of which thinking has need in language is not really what is actually audible to the ear, or, to express it differently, if one resolves articulated sound into articulation and noise, it is not the latter, but only the former.
Articulation rests on the power of the mind over the organs of speech, compelling them to a treatment of tone which corresponds to the form of its working.

That in which this form and articulation meet, as in a connecting means, is that both resolve their domain into fundamental parts whose joining together forms nothing but wholes of such a kind as carry within themselves the striving to become parts of new wholes.

Besides that power, however, there is also in the mind an urge, communicating itself to the organs of speech themselves, to make such use of them, and on that power and this urge rests the production of language even independently of noise audible to the ear.
That language is really wholly inward, and remains possible even without the production and hearing of sound, is taught by the example of deaf-mutes.

Every access to them through the ear is closed; but they learn to understand what is spoken from the movement of the organs of speech of the person speaking and from writing, and they themselves speak when the position and movement of their organs of speech are guided.

This can happen only through the faculty of articulation dwelling in them also, in that, through the connexion of their thinking with their organs of speech, they learn in another person to divine the one member, his thinking, from the other member, the movement of his organs of speech.
The tone that we hear reveals itself to them through the position and movement of the organs; they perceive its articulation without its noise.

Something sensible may also correspond to the latter in them, perhaps something supplied by their imagination in place of what is lacking, of which we have no concept, but always a remarkable resolution of articulated sound takes place in them.
They really understand language, since they read and write alphabetically and themselves learn to speak, not merely thought through signs or pictures.

They learn this not merely because they possess reason, like other human beings, but quite properly because they also possess a capacity for language, a correspondence of their thinking with their organs of speech, and an urge to let both work together, the one and the other essentially grounded in human nature, even if mutilated on one side.

Articulation, however (whose concept I take here only according to its effect, as that shaping of sound which makes it a bearer of thoughts), has in what precedes been described only according to its logical, or at least only according to its intellectual, nature.
In its essential nature, however, it depends precisely on tone as noise, or rather on that vibration of the air through which the organs of speech act at a distance.

It can therefore never be applied immediately to other senses than the ear, and however one might attempt it, one would always produce only signs of tones, not immediately signs of words resolvable into elements.

This rests on the fact that precisely the vibration of the air, audible to another person's ear, through the organs determined by thought is inseparably connected with human nature, and is necessary to its development.
But herein lie three things: the urge of thought towards utterance, the need of feeling for the animal cry, and the necessity of social interaction for the formation of thought.
Each of these items leads singly to the production of tone, and language unites all of them in articulated sound.
Thinking is a mental action, but through its need of language it becomes an impulse to a bodily one.

It is a progressive unfolding, a mere inward movement in which nothing enduring, constant or at rest can be assumed, and at the same time a longing from darkness towards light, from limitation towards infinity.

In the human being, fused into one from a twofold nature, this striving also goes outwards and finds, through the mediation of the organs of speech, in air, the finest and most easily movable of all elements, whose apparent incorporeality also sensibly corresponds to the mind, a material wonderfully suited to it, in which, with the upright posture of man, speech streams freely and calmly from the lips to the ear, which brings hither the light of the stars, and which extends, without visible bounds, into infinity.
In that mental striving thus breaks its way through the lips, its product returns to one's own ear; the subjective inward action is taken up again as an outward object.
Thereby language shares and promotes the innermost nature of thinking, the constant passing over of subject and object into each other.
For no genus of representations can be regarded as a pure contemplation of an object already present.

The activity of the senses must combine synthetically with the inward action of the mind, and from this combination representation tears itself loose, becomes, over against the subjective power, an object, and, perceived anew as such, returns into that power.
Without therefore looking at all to communication between human being and human being, speaking is a necessary condition of the thinking of the individual in secluded solitude.
In appearance, however, language develops only socially.
For man understands himself only in that he has tried and tested the intelligibility of his words on others.

When unarticulated sound takes the place of language, as always in animals and sometimes in man, either need wrings it out, as in adverse feelings, or intention underlies it, in that it lures, warns or calls hither for help, or it streams forth, without need and intention, from the glad feeling of existence, from delight in the loud ringing out of tones.
The last is the poetic element, a spark glimmering up in animal dullness.
These different kinds of sounds are very unequally distributed among the more or less mute and richly sounding genera of animals, and to relatively few has the higher and more joyful kind fallen.
It would also be instructive for language, but perhaps impossible, to fathom whence this diversity stems.

That birds alone possess song could perhaps be explained from the fact that they live more freely than all other animals in the element of tone and in its purer regions, if so many genera of them were not, like the animals that walk on the earth, bound to a few uniform sounds.
Into language the same impelling causes pass over: need, intention and delight in speech.
But the last in language also, and principally, relates to thought, and thereby a fourth cause is added, the need for communication and development of ideas and feelings through conversation.
It certainly belongs to the most erroneous assertions to ascribe the origin of languages pre-eminently to the need of mutual assistance.
Man in the state of nature is not so needy, and for that purpose, as one sees in animals, unarticulated sounds would have sufficed.
Language is, even in its beginnings, thoroughly human.

The languages of the so-called savages too, and precisely they, possess a fullness and manifoldness of expressions everywhere overshooting need, and there is probably in no wilderness a wandering family that does not possess its songs, for man, as an animal genus, is essentially a singing creature, only combining ideas with the tones.
The far more essential ground of the origin of language is delight in speaking, and hence it is of such important influence on the formation of languages how silent or talkative a people is.

Man must always be considered, even in his noblest endeavours, in his whole nature, one side of which he shares with animality, and hence in language too one must not overlook the mere sounding through which, as it were, the animal sound passes over into the articulated sound.
Here the relation of this sounding to the designation of ideas is now first noteworthy.
This can be compared with colouring in painting.
Languages are in this respect now richer, now poorer, now freer from blaring noise, now more overloaded with it.

But it also happens that languages in general, or at certain stages of formation, mix more or less idea-less blaring into real language, use syllables and even words without determinate effect on the sense, almost only for filling out the tone.
A certain feeling may indeed combine with all things of this kind, but this is also possible in the case of unarticulated sound.

Through the cultivation of language these mere filling-out words now either fall away, or, in the more favourable case, become through more artful elaboration signs of finer nuances of ideas or of their combinations.
In the nature of tone as such there finally lies alone the true individuality of every language.

Whatever one may do and attempt to describe its peculiarities, one only ever determines more and more closely the genus to which it belongs; as this and no other language it utters itself only itself before the ear.

Although the alphabet of the whole of mankind is enclosed by certain limits that are not even very wide, yet every people with a language of its own also has its own system of sounds in the exclusion of certain tones, preference for others, determination of the different ones for the designation of different concepts, treatment of the tones in their combinations, and so forth.
One can compare this with the diverse crying and the kinds of tone of the animal genera.
There is in it, even if progressive development rounds much off, something firm, tribal in kind, deeply grounded in the modifications of the organs of speech and in the feeling for tone.

It distinguishes, however, tribes even more than languages, since in the same language individual tribes have tones wholly deviating from all the rest, as for example the Florentines have the breathing guttural sound.

But apart from such details, which appear accidental for language in itself, the system of sounds has the most significant influence on the most essential parts of every language; it is the first thing in which one must establish oneself thoroughly.

This does indeed lead into a laborious elementary investigation often descending into the petty, but it is also nothing but details petty in themselves on which the total impression of languages rests, and nothing is so incompatible with the study of them as wanting to seek out in them merely what is great, mental and predominant.

Exact attention to every grammatical subtlety, and splitting words into their elements, is thoroughly necessary if one does not want to expose oneself to errors in all judgements about structure and even about descent.
The most important cause from which language, by means of tone, needs outward effect is sociability, to which man is unconditionally directed by his nature.

But in it there lies a twofold element, although closely united in a third and higher one: first, that all human powers develop perfectly only socially; that there is something common in the whole human race of which every individual possesses a determination carrying within itself the desire for completion through the others.
Both are especially important precisely in the case of language.

For the greater and more animated the social co-operation upon it is, the more it gains, other circumstances being equal, and on that common element just mentioned rests the possibility of all understanding.
Sociability too cannot without one-sidedness be derived from mere need.
It does not even in animals rest on that.
No animal is easily so sufficient to itself in its strength as the elephant, which lives precisely pre-eminently in herds.
In animals too, therefore, the inclination to sociability, greater in some genera and lesser in others, arises from causes lying much deeper in their being.
It is only impossible for us to fathom them, because we can form no concept at all of the capacity of animals, which is nevertheless not to be denied, to perceive, to feel and to combine perceptions.

In man, however, thinking is essentially bound to social existence, and man needs, apart from all bodily and feeling relations, for mere thinking a Thou corresponding to the I; the concept attains its determinateness and clarity only through being reflected back from a foreign power of thought.
It is produced in that it tears itself loose from the moved mass of representing and forms itself, over against the subject, into an object.

It is not sufficient, however, that this division takes place in the subject alone; objectivity is only completed when the representing person really beholds the thought outside himself, which is possible only in another being representing and thinking like him.
Between power of thought and power of thought, however, the sole mediatress is language, and so here too its necessity for the completion of thought arises.
But there also lies in language itself an unalterable dualism, and all speaking is set upon address and reply.

The word is not an object; rather, over against objects, it is something subjective, but now in the mind of the thinking person it is nevertheless to be an object, produced by him and reacting upon him.
In order that it may now distinguish itself from a mere apparent object, a dream-image, it must gain real being in a person hearing and replying.
The pronoun expresses this original type of all languages through the distinction of the second person from the third.
I and He are really different objects, and with them everything is really exhausted, for in other words they are called I and Non-I.
Thou, however, is a He placed over against the I.
Whereas I and He rest on inner and outer perception, in the Thou there lies spontaneity of choice.
It too is a Non-I, but not, like He, in the sphere of all beings, but in another sphere, that of a common acting through mutual influence.
In the He itself there now thereby lies, besides the Non-I, also a Non-Thou, and it is opposed not merely to one of them, but to both.

That the same pronominal form runs through all languages shows that, according to the feeling of all peoples, speaking in its essence presupposes that the speaker distinguishes, over against himself, a person addressed from all others.

In several American languages a special care to single out the second person even shows itself in this, that they also indicate in the first person of the plural through different forms whether the person addressed is included under it or excluded from it.
What results in this way when one attempts to analyse the simple act of thinking repeats itself incessantly in the mental life of man; social communication affords him conviction and stimulation.
The power of thought needs something equal to it and yet separated from it.
Through what is equal it is kindled; through what is separated from it it receives a touchstone of the real being of its inner productions.

For man in his changeable limitation can regard truth, as what is fixed without bounds, only as lying outside himself, and his whole mental striving is a wrestling towards it, and the mightiest means of coming near to it, of measuring his distance from it, is social union.
Thus language is a necessary requirement for the first production of thought and for the progressive formation of the mind.
Mental communication, passing over from the one to the other, presupposes in the latter something common to him with the former.
One understands the heard word only because one could oneself have said it.

Nothing can be present in the soul except through its own activity, and understanding is just as much as speaking itself a stimulation of the power of language, only in its inner receptivity, as speaking is in its outer activity, hence it is also so natural for man at once to utter again what he has just understood.

Hence there lies in every human being language in its whole extent, which, however, means nothing else than that everyone possesses a striving, regulated by a determinately modified power impelling and limiting, gradually to produce the whole language, as outer or inner occasion brings it about, or to understand it when produced.

This power is, like every power, naturally an individual one, but individualized according to all the generic concepts by virtue of which every genus can be taken, in relation to a more general and higher one, as an individual.

It is therefore the general power of language, determined by the tribal stock, the nation, the dialect, then fixed in its sound-signs, determined in the manner of use by all inner qualities and outer accidents acting so powerfully on the inner mind that the effect becomes perceptible in language, and finally by the individuality that can no longer be brought under any more general category.

Each of these stages, ascending to the most general, forms a sphere of language, which is determined by what is common to everything comprised under it and by what is different from what is situated outside it.

In every general investigation of language it therefore becomes a necessary task, at the various points coming into consideration, for example in the alphabet, to seek out the limits of human language in general, in this wide domain to separate off the smaller domains, again comprised within one another, of the individual genera of language, and everywhere to see whether these fulfil the concept from which the division is made, and thus in their historical existence form a whole given through the idea.

Every multiplicity of what is in itself of the same kind brings this task with it, and pre-eminently in investigations which, like those concerning language, are conducted not merely in order historically to know and present, but teleologically so as to react formatively upon language and man.
The general connexion of languages is indeed explained by the sameness of kind of human nature, in which similar powers act according to the same laws.

A deeper investigation and fuller appreciation of language seems to me, however, to lead much further, and to a point to which I have hitherto wished only to clear the way through easier considerations, and at which no further explanation is possible, just as no metaphysical investigation, that is, one grounded on fathoming being in itself, can lead further than to the end of what is to be explained.

Now to me — for I utter this preferably in the tone of inner conviction rather than with the confidence of general assertion — the essence of language seems to be misconceived, the mental process of its origin (not that in itself, but also that in each act of speaking and understanding) only apparently explained, and its powerful effect on the inner mind incorrectly appreciated, if one regards the human race as countless natures belonging to the same genus, and not rather as One nature split into countless individuals, a view to which one also arrives in wholly other relations than that of language, and from wholly other points.

The difference between the two assertions placed opposite each other is evident, since the inner relationship of the human race according to the latter rests on the unity of its being, according to the former only on the unity of the idea which, contemplating or creating, comprehends it.
In the manner of this relationship lies locked the mystery of human individuality, which can at the same time be regarded as the mystery of human existence.

It is the point at which, in a state following the earthly one, a difference may pre-eminently be expected, which then, if consciousness connected both states, would at the same time produce a thoroughgoing alteration of all previous views.

This mystery cannot be explained and fathomed, but for the correct explanation of appearances and for the direction of intellectual striving one must beware of misconceiving the true being of that relationship of human individuality, of drawing it merely from logical and discursive concepts, and of not rather apprehending it from the depth of inner feeling and in a reflection that pursues the investigation to its end-points.
One therefore already gains if one lets the view indicated in what precedes as the correct one stand even only as a divined possibility, and does not shut oneself up in the opposite view.

What speaks most convincingly for me against the latter view is what was said above: that understanding too rests wholly on inner self-activity, and speaking with one another is only a mutual awakening of the power of language present in the hearer.
The conceiving of words is thoroughly different from the understanding of unarticulated sounds, and comprehends far more in itself than the mere mutual evoking of sound and indicated object.

The word can indeed also be taken as an indivisible whole, just as in writing one may well recognize the sense of a group of words without yet being certain of its alphabetical composition, and it would be possible that the child's soul proceeded in this way in the first beginnings of understanding.

But as soon as not merely the animal faculty of feeling but the human power of language is stimulated (and there may well be no moment even in the child at which this, however weakly, is not the case), the word is also perceived as articulated.

Now what articulation adds to the mere evoking of its meaning (which naturally also takes place through it in higher perfection) is that it presents the word immediately through its form as a part of an infinite whole, a language.

For through it the possibility is given, even in individual words, of forming from their elements a number of other words really extending to infinity, according to determining feelings and rules, and thereby establishing among all words a relationship corresponding to the relationship of the concepts.

The soul would, however, receive no divination at all of this artful mechanism, and would conceive articulation as little as the blind man conceives colour, if a power to bring that possibility into actuality did not dwell in it.

Children's learning to speak is not a measuring out of words, laying them down in the memory and repeating them babblingly with the lips, but a growth of the faculty of language through age and practice.

What is heard does more than merely communicate itself; it disposes the soul to understand more easily also what has not yet been heard, makes clear things heard long ago but then half or not at all understood, in that their sameness of kind with what has just been perceived suddenly becomes evident to the power that has since become sharper, and sharpens the urge and the faculty of drawing ever more and more quickly from what is heard over into understanding, of letting ever less of it rush past as mere sound.

Progress therefore also does not take place, as for instance in learning vocabulary, in a uniform proportion growing only through strengthened practice of memory, but in a constantly self-intensifying one, since the heightening of power and the gaining of material mutually strengthen and extend each other.

That in children not a mechanical learning of language but a development of the power of language takes place is also proved by the fact that to all human powers a certain point in age is assigned for their development, and that under the most diverse circumstances all children speak and understand at approximately the same age, varying only within a short period.

But how could the hearer, merely through the growth of his developing power, gain such strength as to master what is spoken, if there were not in the speaker and the hearer the same being, only individually and mutually appropriately separated, so that so fine a sign, yet drawn precisely from the deepest and fullest nature of that being, as articulated sound is, suffices, mediatingly, to stimulate both in concordant manner?
If this is correct, it at the same time becomes clear how separation and mixing of nations become the cause of the diversity of their languages.

For the further human beings diverge from one another thereby, the more the separation of individuality sets itself against the unity of being, although the unity of human nature in general also proves itself in this, that children of every people, transferred from the mother's lap into any foreign one, develop their faculty of language in the language of the latter.

This appearance can indeed also be adduced in precisely the opposite direction, to show that speaking is merely a reproducing of what is heard and depends on intercourse without regard to unity or diversity of being.

But however much one must attribute to the even predominant power of the surrounding sounds, it would be arbitrary to want to deny the influence of descent, which in these extraordinary cases is only suppressed.

It already exerts an undeniable influence on the vocal organs, which must indeed be individually modified, and modified naturally in accordance with the language of the fathers, and now, in appropriating and resisting, mix this modification into every effect upon them.
But nothing stands so isolated in man, and the intellectual faculty of language too certainly knows just such a tribal disposition.

That the language of one's fatherland possesses for the educated and the uneducated a far greater strength and intimacy than a foreign one, that after long deprivation it greets the ear with a kind of sudden magic and in distant places touches it with longing, and that this rests not at all on the mental element in it, the expressed thought or feeling, but precisely on the inexplicable, most individual element, on its sound, might well also speak for that real unity of being.
It is as if with the native sound one perceived a part of one's self from the other person.

If one only pays sufficient attention to appearances of this kind, individuals can also be shown, in the finest and most mental use of language, in the literature of nations, who, estranged from childhood from their language, which they did not learn at all, nevertheless always mixed something into the use of the appropriated language by which it showed itself that their original determination for another language had, against the nature of their being, been accidentally displaced.
Meanwhile, even without any influence of descent, peculiar dialects arise merely through intercourse and common life.

This is found pre-eminently within the circle of real national languages among individual classes of the people, and the peculiar dialects of women, so frequent especially in the American languages, as well as those of the different estates in Malay, are of this kind.
But common descent can also be added, as in the language of the Incas, which was at the same time a family language and a language of estate.
In all these cases the principle is, as in language-formation in general, community that separates itself off, accidentally or intentionally.

In what precedes, presenting language as the organ of thinking, we have considered articulated sound, which constitutes its essence, according to its twofold nature, as articulation (21.) and as sound (22 — 38.).

If we now turn to what is produced through speaking, or rather through thinking in language, we find there too that the mode of representation according to which language merely designates perceived objects, whose total mass we call the world, is far removed from exhausting its deep and full content.
Just as little as a concept is possible without it, just as little can there be an object for the soul without it, since every external object receives real being for it only by means of the concept.
Into the formation and use of language there necessarily passes the whole manner of the subjective perception of objects.
For the word arises precisely from this perception, and is not an impression of the object in itself, but of the image produced by the latter in the soul.
Since subjectivity is unavoidably mixed into all objective perception, every human individuality can already, independently of language, be regarded as a peculiar standpoint of the view of the world.

It becomes so, however, far more through language, since the word, over against the soul, also makes itself in turn into an object and brings in a new peculiarity separating itself off from the subject, so that now in the concept there lies a threefold element: the impression of the object, the manner of the reception of it in the subject, and the effect of the word as a language-sound.

In this last element there necessarily reigns in the same language a thoroughgoing analogy, and since now a subjectivity of the same kind also acts upon language in the same nation, there lies in every language a peculiar view of the world.
This expression in no way exceeds the measure of simple truth.

For the connexion of all parts of language with one another, and of the whole language with the nation, is so close that, if once this interaction indicates a determinate direction, thoroughgoing peculiarity must necessarily arise from it.

But language is a view of the world not merely because it, since every concept is to be capable of being grasped through it, must equal the extent of the world, but also because only the transformation that it undertakes with objects makes the mind capable of insight into the connexion inseparable from the concept of the world.
Man also lives chiefly with objects as language supplies them to him, and, since feeling and acting in him depend on his representations, he lives even exclusively so.

Through the same act by virtue of which man spins language out of himself, he spins himself into it, and every language draws around the nation to which it belongs a circle from which it is possible to go out only in so far as one at the same time steps over into the circle of another language.

The learning of a foreign language, used in the right manner, is therefore the gaining of a new standpoint in the previous view of the world, since every language contains the whole web of concepts and of the mode of representation of a part of mankind.
I have hitherto treated more of speaking than of language, and have chiefly described the production and understanding of speech and the influence that it exerts on the soul.

From speaking, however, language produces itself, a stock of words and a system of rules, and grows, winding itself through the succession of millennia, into a power in a certain manner independent of the person speaking at any given time, of the generation at any given time, of the nation, and finally even of mankind.
In what precedes we have become aware that the thought taken up into language becomes an object for the soul and exerts on it an effect coming to it to that extent as something foreign.
But we have considered the object pre-eminently as having arisen from the subject, and the effect as having proceeded from that upon which it reacts.
Now the opposite view enters, according to which language really is a foreign object and its effect really has proceeded from something other than that upon which it acts.

For language must necessarily (31.) belong to two, and in fact it belongs to the whole human race; since now it also in writing preserves slumbering thought in a state in which it can be awakened by the mind, it forms for itself a peculiar existence which, though it can always receive validity only in thinking at any given time, is in its totality independent of that thinking.

The two opposite views suggested here, that language is foreign to the soul and belongs to it, is independent of it and dependent on it, really combine in it and constitute the peculiarity of its being.
This conflict must also not be resolved in such a way that language is partly foreign and independent and partly neither.
Language is object and independent precisely in so far as it is subject and dependent.

For it has nowhere, not even in writing, an enduring place, but must always be produced anew in thinking and consequently pass wholly into the subject; but it lies in the act of this production to make it precisely just as much into an object; on this path it experiences each time the whole influence of the individual, but this influence is already in itself bound by what language effects and has effected.
The true resolution of that opposition lies in the unity of human nature adduced above (34.).
In that which stems from what is really one with me, the concepts of subject and object, of dependence and independence, pass over into each other.
Language belongs to me because I produce it.

It does not belong to me because I cannot produce it otherwise than I do, and since the ground of this lies in the speaking and having spoken of all human generations, in so far as linguistic communication may have existed among them without interruption, it is language itself from which I experience this limitation.

The foreign influence to which man is subject in the use of language is, however, besides that of language just mentioned, given the close connexion of language with his whole remaining being, also that which descent, surrounding situation and manner of common life exert upon that being.

This is pre-eminently important in historical investigations of language, since on the one side one must beware of explaining a language wholly from the circumstances acting upon the nation, and on the other side must not forget that even a language historically and undeniably handed down can suffer through the nation alterations that seem incredible.
It is with this twofold series of linked effects that one has to do everywhere in investigations of language.

For, like all things historically concerning the human race, they always place one only in a middle of things, and wanting to think a beginning, or even to explain one, would lead to empty presuppositions.

Even there, therefore, where neither history nor tradition gives knowledge of an earlier state and shows a more general connexion, one must always regard it as a task for attention directed everywhere to find some such connexion.

If one considers how everything that the language of a people has experienced through all preceding centuries acts bindingly upon the generation at any given time in that people, and how only the power of the individual generation comes into contact with it, and this not even purely, since the rising and the departing generation live intermixed beside each other, it becomes clear how small the power of the individual really is against the might of language.

Only through the uncommon pliability of language, through the possibility, of which I shall speak further below, of taking up its forms in very different ways without detriment to general understanding, and through the power which everything living and mental exerts over what is handed down dead, is the equilibrium to some extent restored again.
Yet it is always language in which every individual feels that he is nothing but an outflow of the whole human race.
Only because everyone nevertheless individually and incessantly reacts upon it does every generation nevertheless produce a change in it, which in many cases evades observation.

For the change can be twofold, one in the words and forms themselves and one in the differently modified use of them, and the latter is, where writing and literature are lacking, partly smaller and partly more difficult to perceive.

Since what exists is always changed, and always only by an individual power wrestling against an infinite mass, it already follows from this of itself that every change in language, and also the origin of new languages, takes place only gradually.

Nations too, which through the change of centuries go hand in hand with languages, arise in no other way, and the means through which all new languages (in so far as we can recognize them) are formed are estrangement and admixture.
A body of a tribe branches off and settles where it either encounters no one as yet, or mixes with another tribe.

There can be no talk of invention of a language in the domain of historical investigation of language, and the expressions that a people creates its language, that it proceeds from its individuality, even that it belongs to it exclusively, need caution in order to be used correctly.

The very same is the case with the application of the concept of descent to languages, which must never be taken as if one language in its totality could proceed from another, but only in the sense that the alleged mother language has, in the mouth of generations that separated themselves off and mixed with foreign ones, transformed itself into a daughter language.

But since in this way several languages pass over into a new one, the application of this concept already misleads in this respect, that it makes one seek a parent language, whereas all the different materials of the language to be investigated ought to be separated.

Nations themselves are just as little purely separated from one another, but also flow over into one another and form themselves gradually through the co-operating principle of separation and holding together; only the peculiarity thus arising becomes visible at a certain point only after formation is completed.
Mr Klaproth already remarks this in the Asia polyglotta. P. [43.]
All languages of peoples between whom any connexion has ever prevailed must therefore be regarded as One language, altered only through estrangement and mixing into manifold subspecies.

This is a principal principle in every investigation of language, equally important for examining etymologically the sameness of kind of languages and for presenting philosophically the manner in which language spreads over the human race.

It rests, however, on the simple and undeniable fact that where human beings who have hitherto lived wholly separated visit one another or unite with one another, [they] gradually alter their original speaking and transform it into a new one upon which they unite, usually both, but sometimes also only one, the one overpowered by the other first bodily, then mentally.
Even if the original speaking remains separated, individual words and forms nevertheless pass over reciprocally.
Etymologically, therefore, one has to seek out the different elements of a language and their relation.

Only if all elements were of the same kind and concordant with the language of another people, that is, if the language had arisen merely through branching off, without any mixture, could the concept of descent fit.
But since it always at the same time includes earlier and later existence in itself, it can almost never be decided from language alone.
Philosophically it now matters to investigate what in language man holds most firmly to, and what diversity he enters into more easily and more difficultly.

By the unity of several languages expressed in the principle just set up, the unity of an original language is by no means meant, but this, that every language carries in itself some element that also belongs to another, and, because this is the case with all, all are mediately altered and affected through one another.

To regard the different languages as parts (dialects), existing beside one another, of one language embracing all, not as having arisen from one another in time, is the peculiarity of that assertion, which moreover carries with it no pretension to novelty at all, but has only the purpose, by cutting off untimely comparisons, of determining concepts more firmly and bringing them more into accord with the facts.

The temporal succession of languages too must not be neglected in their study; it is only not to be mixed in unsuitably, and since the beginning of most languages still existing loses itself in darkness, in this ignorance of their temporal succession there arises for us in a certain measure a simultaneity of them.
To assume an original language, or to set up a diversity of languages before and after the extermination of the greatest part of the human race through a flood, seems to me useless and misleading.
Neither the domain of facts nor that of pure concepts can lead to that.

There may have been one, there may have been several original languages, in the strictest sense if the human race has more than one geographical starting-point, in a less strict sense if — and precisely great floods could bring this about — peoples had become so isolated that every trace of their earlier connexion had been lost in their language.
But facts to be drawn from languages will hardly prove the one or the other, and for the explanation of appearances in language one will hardly need either the one assumption or the other.

The concept of an original language, however, if one does not want to infer anything in particular from it, can indeed as little be rejected as that of any beginning of the human race, and so it can also happen, in relation to the principle set up above (44.), that a branched-off body of a people mixes with one upon which none of the languages standing in connexion with the former has ever acted, not even in the most mediate way.
Two such tribal stocks would then, if one follows the succession of generations upwards, indeed connect their language to two original languages.

Everywhere where real intercourse of speakers has existed among peoples, however mediate it may be, sameness of kind of their languages arises from language already formed; and conversely, if such sameness of kind arising from formed language can be recognized in languages, it proves such an intercourse.

This is important because thereby at least, even if it should be of little fruitfulness for application, the principle is expressed according to which the historical connexion of languages can be distinguished from that sameness of kind which is to be sought merely in the sameness of kind of human dispositions.

For suppose that the American nations had had a native origin and, until the spread of the languages still existing, had mixed with no inhabitants of the rest of the earth, then no non-American sound would have been heard in America, and thus there could be no sameness of kind between the American languages and the other languages of the earth that had arisen through language already formed.

Nevertheless the general dispositions of man would still be the same in America too; there would be, whether one derives them from descent from one human pair or from the unity of the creating idea, the same unity of human being without which (34.) language itself would not be possible; hence a sameness of kind of languages would also necessarily have to proceed from that.
In this sense there is only One language, as there is only One human genus, and all difference of races abolishes neither the concept of humanity nor the possibility of regular propagation.

This becomes still more evident if one considers that also the surroundings of nature acting upon man, and therefore also upon language, are in large measure the same, and the means of which all languages make use, as tones, are enclosed within not very wide limits.

In languages of historical connexion too this general sameness of kind occurs, but only in those parts upon which the foreign sounds that have been added have not acted, yet never purely, since in language, which has its existence merely in the activity of production at any given time (40.), every influence always penetrates the whole.

Whether there may now be sufficient means of distinguishing in the languages themselves this possible twofold sameness of kind may for now remain undecided; but it was necessary to determine it exactly according to its concept.

We shall in what follows have to return very fully to this point, since America could more easily than any part of the old world (unless one wanted perhaps to except central Africa) have remained free from every mixture with foreigners.
In all languages, therefore, one encounters what is of the same kind, and the hope of finding in any one of them something wholly new would be vain.
I do not deny that the great similarity of the European and of several Asiatic languages first drove me to the study of the American ones.

I believed that I should there come upon a wholly foreign domain, and at first sight, and in a certain measure, it is so too, but closer examination shows the appearances there too to be less foreign in kind.
The task in the investigation of every language is therefore recognition of what is characteristic within sameness of kind.

For since language is always One, that is, since everything thought in language always proceeds in the moment at any given time from the whole language (or, if this seems clearer, the whole linguistic proficiency) of the individual, and therefore the whole language expresses itself in this individual utterance, what is of the same kind does not subsist beside what is characteristic, but passes over into it, that is, the general power dwelling in the whole human race determines itself individually.

Sameness of kind and individuality can therefore be separated only in idea, and, although what is individual, as the immediate fact, can merely be perceived and not be presented in analysed form for the understanding, one must nevertheless apprehend both as far as possible in their unity.

I should not wish what I have just said about the appearance of the whole language in everything individually spoken to be taken for one of those exaggerations to which one easily runs the risk of abandoning oneself in general reasonings stripped of examples.
It is meant thereby to express that in language everything is determined through each thing and each thing through everything, and this is literally true.

In the simplest sentence one can even factually demonstrate a great part of this connexion if one resolves the sentence into its elements according to all kinds of analysis possible in languages, brings every element into all the categories that correspond to it, compares it there with those comprised with it in the same category, and thereupon compares the categories themselves with one another, and so continues ever further to go through all determining relations of language and to investigate how the determination prevailing in each also determines the element of the given sentence.
Infinitely much, however, admittedly rests on analogies of linguistic feeling that cannot be presented.

It results of itself from what precedes that, although the individual language-sound is the last real appearance, the individuality of a language must nevertheless not be sought merely in its tone, nor what is of the same kind perhaps in the ideal element.
Individuality rather shows itself in everything, and is one and the same from the alphabet to the world-representation (39.) in the totality of language.
As those fundamental tones would be differently posited, so would this mode of viewing also be different, and conversely.
No one will demand that this should really be presented in any language.

This is indeed impossible, but the matter is nevertheless true and important on that account; true because it follows necessarily from the nature of speaking and of language developed in what precedes, important because, if one departs from the two fundamental truths of all investigation of language — that language constitutes one whole with the entire thinking and feeling of man, and that it has existence nowhere except in the eternally mutually generating act of speaking and thinking in language — because, if one departs from these, I say, one also overlooks what can in fact be recognized in real languages.
Pre-eminently, however, the proper widening of the outlook upon languages is necessary for their correct treatment.

Since everything in language is mental, it depends on the energy and intelligence that makes use of language how strongly and fully it acts upon thinking and feeling, and every more correct insight into it becomes alive in the whole human being in the purer influence of its individuality.

In one's own use, however, everything also enters into feeling, and thus into knowledge, that can never be presented through the analysing understanding, and so from use guided by a widened survey there also arises widened insight.
What one has felt in one's own language, however deep and fine it may be, one divines more easily in a foreign one.

Thus it is probably undeniable that, since the principal nations of Europe began to write in their mother tongues, a wholly different insight has arisen from what existed before into the connexion which each of them has within itself and with the nation.

This epoch, which I regard as the most important in the treatment of language, is also distinguished by this, and in our time it acts much more powerfully than the same appearance did among the ancients, since among them only two languages, among us, however, several, entered into contact, and into much more actively rivalrous contact.

In order, however, to leave nothing lacking in the sharp delimitation of concepts, it must still be added to what precedes that the individuality of a language can also be a unity only comparatively, and that true individuality lies only in the person speaking at any given time.
In fact only this completes the concept.
A nation indeed has on the whole the same language, but already not all its members (38.) have quite the same, and if one goes still further into what is finest, every human being possesses his own.
No one thinks at a word exactly what another does, and the difference, however small, trembles, if one wants to compare language with the most movable of all elements, through the whole language.
In every act of thinking and feeling the same difference returns by virtue of the sameness of individuality, and forms a mass out of things individually imperceptible.

All understanding is therefore always at the same time a not-understanding, a truth that can also be excellently used in practical life; all agreement in thoughts and feelings is at the same time a going apart.

This becomes visible only where it does not hide itself under the generality of concept and feeling; but where heightened power breaks through generality and individualizes more sharply also for consciousness, there it comes clearly to light.
Thus no one will deny every significant writer his own language.

It can indeed be objected that by language one understands only precisely that generality of forms, words and rules which allows room precisely for diverse individuality, and this is indeed completely true.
Nevertheless the view suggested cannot on that account be banished from the domain even of the most general investigation of language.

For there are several stages on which the generality of linguistic forms individualizes itself in this way, and the individualizing principle is the same: thinking and speaking in a determinate individuality.
Thereby arises the diversity in the language of individuals as of nations.
Everywhere it is only a more or less.
One must therefore descend to the last stage.
One might indeed want to find the boundary where language, even if individually nuanced, nevertheless makes use of the same sounds.

But even this is already not quite the case with the different classes of a nation, and the individual too uses some sounds pre-eminently, makes use of others as if they were foreign to him, excludes still others wholly, and thereby forms for himself, apart from the deviations in meaning, his own dictionary.

Pre-eminently, however, it is necessary to draw attention to the modification of language in every individual in order to prove the power of man over language, just as in what precedes (42. 43.) we have presented its might over him.

The latter can be regarded (if one wants to apply the expression to mental powers) as a physiological working; the former is a purely dynamical one; in the latter lies the nature of the working powers of language, in the former the principle of its freedom.

For something can arise in man whose ground no understanding can discover in preceding states, and one would misconceive the nature of language, and precisely violate the historical truth of its origin and alteration, if one wanted to exclude the possibility of such inexplicable appearances from it.

But even if freedom is indeterminable and inexplicable, its limits can be recognized, though only within a certain latitude, and investigation of language must recognize and honour the appearance of freedom, but carefully trace its limits, so as not to regard as possible through freedom in languages what is not so.

Nations also alter their languages constantly merely through themselves, without branching off and mixture, in their common continuing life, and after larger periods these alterations become noticeable.
Extent, rapidity and manner of these alterations depend on the liveliness of linguistic intercourse and on the depth with which man grasps the content of language.
For we shall see further below that in this respect there are different degrees.
To pay attention to these alterations is a principal business of research into language.

But also where language is more violently transformed through branching off and mixture, national individuality acts pre-eminently according to the manner in which what is foreign touches it, and in which it works upon the foreign element with the power dwelling in it.

There is, however, hardly need of the reminder that, in order to make this national influence clear to oneself, one must go back to that peculiar treatment of language by the individual which appears in it only as a mass.

But also within a nation an individual sometimes deviates from the course given through all, and through a view suddenly lighting up in him, through a decisive invention, or through his peculiar manner of using language, makes a new manner of treating language prevail.
For although limits are set to the intellectuality of nations, just as to that of the human race, a certain latitude nevertheless remains reserved to the individual even there.

Everywhere where freedom moves within bounds of finitude there is indeed a series of determining influences foreign to it at the moment of working, but it can also, like lightning from the cloudless ether, suddenly step out of them and become self-determining.

On this it rests that in mankind and in the deeply moved human being an incessant creating is alive, that the manner of their being can never be either calculated or exhaustively explained, since the inexplicable principle of freedom remains mixed into every direction.

In languages it comes from this that they take unexpected sudden flights upward, and do not even always gradually sink down, that languages in themselves of the same kind experience such different treatment among different nations, that they show great diversity of character, as for example Greek and Latin, and that individual writers found wholly new epochs in the manner of treating them, which certainly also happened before the invention of writing, only there it loses itself in darkness for posterity.

This consideration becomes important for research into language pre-eminently because a warning is to be found in it against the sufficiency of merely mechanical kinds of explanation and against too great trust in analytical procedure.

It must indeed trace the uniform course that man takes in altering and forming language, but only with regard to the independent power that can leave that course or shorten it, whose mere breath gives linguistic materials a wholly different nature; one must indeed analyse and derive one thing from another, but only with the feeling that there are also true syntheses, where idea and sound meet on a path that cannot be further investigated.

Just as the stock of words and the system of rules that we call language are always made fruitful by the living mind in thinking, speaking and recording, so investigation too must always have the living mind and dead language at the same time before its eyes and follow their interaction.
The individuality of nations can take such manifold paths that every attempt to grasp it even only in genera would be in vain.

But for the principal influences upon language it always matters only to know the two points: whether it inclines at all, and from which side, to intellectuality, and whether it inclines precisely to intellectuality through language?

For just as in daily life one encounters different degrees and kinds of need for language, feeling for language and treatment of language among human beings, so it is also with nations, and what appears in the constant further formation of languages also happened in their arising from one another, since this itself (43.) could only be a gradual becoming different.

Much more could be remarked about this diversity of national appropriation of language if it were not my purpose in this chapter, in order to show the structure and the interlocking of the whole, merely to touch on particulars by way of indication.

Since we have now considered language in general in its twofold nature, as a mental act in speaking and understanding and as dead material produced through that act, material present indeed never outside man but always outside the individual (40 — 54.), and since we have further separated in it the natural connexion (40 — 51.) from national and individual freedom (52 — 54.), we now pass to its procedure in particulars.
In this procedure two things now clearly separate themselves from each other, words and the combination of speech, as the matter and form of language.

This division must not be confused with that into sounds and rules; for word-formation too knows rules, and the combination of speech sometimes makes use of sounds peculiar to it; rather, regarding speech as the purpose of language, one must hold fast to this classification in its true nature in such a way that the one part treats the elements of speech and the other its combination.
But since sound is common to both, consideration of the system of sounds must be placed in front.
